skill.name: codebase-explorer
skill.description: Explore Empathy Ledger codebase structure, database schema, service layers, API routes, and data-flow relationships.
skill.summary: Map Empathy Ledger architecture, data flows, services, API routes, and database relationships.
skill.author: Acurioustractor

security_audit.summary: The reported issues are false positives caused by markdown inline code, fenced examples, a local API placeholder, and a relative documentation link. No malicious intent, prompt injection, secret exfiltration, destructive command, or runtime path traversal was found in SKILL.md.

remediation.issue: Static scanners may misread markdown code fences and inline paths as executable backtick usage.
remediation.suggestion: Keep examples clearly documented as references, and avoid adding instructions that run untrusted user input in shell commands.

remediation.issue: The skill references a service-role Supabase client that bypasses RLS.
remediation.suggestion: When using this skill, verify any service-role guidance against project authorization rules before suggesting code changes.

content.value_statement: Large codebases make it hard to find the right files and understand data flow. This skill gives Claude, Codex, or Claude Code a focused map of Empathy Ledger services, routes, schema, and relationships.
actual_capabilities: Identifies key database type files for users, organizations, projects, stories, distribution, locations, and analysis.
Explains the expected data flow from React components through API routes, services, Supabase, and PostgreSQL.
Lists core service-layer files and their stated business purposes.
Maps important API route groups for stories, storytellers, projects, embeds, and admin operations.
Summarizes tenant isolation expectations and the project role hierarchy.
Provides safe local exploration commands for finding services, routes, migrations, tables, and components.
limitations: The skill is tailored to the Empathy Ledger repository and may not generalize to other projects.
It is a navigation guide, not a full static analyzer or test runner.
Referenced files may become outdated if the upstream codebase changes.
It does not verify runtime behavior or database policy enforcement by itself.

use_cases.title: Find the right implementation area
use_cases.description: Locate the service, API route, component, or type file that owns a feature before making changes.

use_cases.title: Understand tenant-aware data flow
use_cases.description: Trace how requests should move from UI actions to Supabase while preserving tenant isolation.

use_cases.title: Prepare architecture explanations
use_cases.description: Create concise summaries of database tables, service responsibilities, and route boundaries for planning discussions.

prompt_templates.title: Find a feature area
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the codebase explorer to find where story distribution is implemented. Show the likely service files, API routes, and database tables.

prompt_templates.title: Trace a data flow
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the codebase explorer to trace how a project transcript request should flow from a component to the database. Include route, service, Supabase, and table layers.

prompt_templates.title: Map tenant isolation
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the codebase explorer to explain how tenant isolation should be checked for organization and project data. Identify files I should inspect before editing.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a cross-cutting change
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the codebase explorer to plan where to add a new cultural safety workflow. Cover database types, services, API routes, components, and risks to verify.

output: Start with the consent service because it owns the GDPR consent proof system.
Inspect story consent API routes for request handling and authorization checks.
Review story ownership database types for consent proof and distribution table relationships.

output_examples.input: How does a story request reach the database?
output: A React component calls a local API route.
The API route delegates business rules to a service layer file.
The service uses a Supabase client, then PostgreSQL applies the schema and policies.

output_examples.input: What should I check before editing admin operations?
output: Review admin API routes first, then inspect any service-role client usage.
Confirm tenant and role checks before changing behavior.
Look for audit or compliance logging requirements tied to the operation.

best_practices: Ask for file locations and relationships before requesting edits.
Verify tenant and role boundaries when exploring admin or service-role paths.
Pair this skill with direct file reads when you need current implementation details.
anti_patterns: Do not assume the reference tables are complete after the repository changes.
Do not use the listed commands to modify files without a separate implementation plan.
Do not treat the service-role client as safe for normal user-scoped operations.

faq.question: What does this skill help me find?
faq.answer: It helps locate Empathy Ledger database types, services, API routes, components, and data-flow relationships.

faq.question: Does it edit code automatically?
faq.answer: No. It is a navigation and explanation skill. Code changes require a separate user request.

faq.question: Can it validate database security policies?
faq.answer: No. It can point to tenant isolation patterns, but policy validation needs direct code and database review.

faq.question: Which tools can use it?
faq.answer: The report lists Claude, Codex, and Claude Code as supported tools.

faq.question: Is this useful outside Empathy Ledger?
faq.answer: Only partially. The file paths and architecture notes are specific to Empathy Ledger.

faq.question: Why does it mention service-role access?
faq.answer: It documents where admin Supabase operations may live, so users know to review authorization carefully.
